stem: In which work do we find the first known instance of numbers written using ten digits, including the digit 0 notated as a dot?
options: Yajurveda Samhita
Bakhshali manuscript
Aryabhatiya
Brahmasphutasiddhanta
explanation: Correct option: (B). The Bakhshali manuscript (c. 3rd century CE) is the first known instance of numbers written with ten digits, with zero shown as a dot. The Yajurveda Samhita lists number names based on powers of 10 but is not about written digits; the Aryabhatiya (499 CE) and the Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE) came later.

stem: The word 'algorithm' is named after a Persian mathematician who popularised the Hindu numerals in the Arab world. Who was he?
options: Al-Kindi
Fibonacci
Al-Khwarizmi
Pierre-Simon Laplace
explanation: Correct option: (C). Al-Khwarizmi wrote 'On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals' (c. 825), and the word 'algorithm' comes from his name. Al-Kindi also wrote on Hindu numerals but the word is not named after him; Fibonacci was an Italian who promoted the numerals in Europe; Laplace was a later French scholar who praised the system.

stem: Why did European scholars come to call the Indian numerals 'Arabic numerals'?
options: They learnt the numerals from the Arab world
Arab scholars invented the digits 0 to 9
Arab books always called them by that name
The digits were first written in Arabic script
explanation: Correct option: (A). European scholars learnt the Indian numerals from the Arab world, so from their perspective they called them 'Arabic numerals'. The digits were developed in India, not invented by Arab scholars; Arab scholars such as Al-Khwarizmi and Al-Kindi actually called them 'Hindu numerals'; and the digits were not first written in Arabic script.

stem: Arrange these events in time order: (P) Fibonacci urges Europe to adopt the Indian numerals; (Q) the Bakhshali manuscript is written; (R) Al-Khwarizmi writes his book on Hindu numerals; (S) Aryabhata does elaborate computations with the ten-symbol system.
options: S, Q, R, P
Q, R, S, P
Q, S, P, R
Q, S, R, P
explanation: Correct option: (D). Bakhshali manuscript (c. 3rd century CE), then Aryabhata (c. 499 CE), then Al-Khwarizmi (c. 825 CE), then Fibonacci (around 1200 CE): Q, S, R, P. Putting S first ignores that the Bakhshali manuscript is older; putting R before S places a 9th-century book before a 5th-century mathematician; putting P before R makes Europe adopt the numerals before the Arab world passed them on.

stem: A student argues: 'Europeans called them Arabic numerals, so the digits 0 to 9 must have been invented in Arabia.' Which fact from the chapter most directly shows the argument is wrong?
options: Arab scholars themselves called them 'Hindu numerals'
Fibonacci, who promoted them, was an Italian scholar
Roman numerals stayed in use in Europe for many centuries
The shapes of the digits changed over many centuries
explanation: Correct option: (A). If Arab scholars such as Al-Khwarizmi and Al-Kindi titled their own works 'On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals' and 'On the Use of the Hindu Numerals', the Arab world itself recognised the numerals as coming from India, so the European name reflects only where Europe learnt them. Fibonacci's nationality, the long use of Roman numerals in Europe and the changing shapes of the digits say nothing about where the digits were invented.

stem: A herder keeps one stick for each cow so that no two cows are matched with the same stick. What is this way of matching called?
options: A place value system
A base-n system
A one-to-one mapping
A landmark number
explanation: Correct option: (C). Associating each cow with a stick so that no two cows share the same stick is a one-to-one mapping. A place value system and a base-n system are ways of writing numbers using positions and powers, and a landmark number is a number given its own symbol; none of these describes the matching itself.

stem: According to the chapter, what is a number system?
options: A set of symbols that may be used in any order
A standard sequence that has a fixed order
A collection made up of written symbols only
A list of the names of very large numbers
explanation: Correct option: (B). The chapter defines a number system as a standard sequence of objects, names or written symbols that has a fixed order. Without a fixed order, counting by matching would not work; a number system can use objects or names, not only written symbols; and it is not just a list of names of large numbers.

stem: What is the main limitation of counting by matching objects with the English letters 'a' to 'z', one letter per object?
options: It cannot count more than 26 objects
It needs as many sticks as objects
The letters do not have a fixed order
It cannot count fewer than 26 objects
explanation: Correct option: (A). With one letter per object, the sequence ends at 'z', so collections of more than 26 objects cannot be counted. Needing as many sticks as objects is the drawback of Method 1, not Method 2; the alphabet does have a fixed order; and fewer than 26 objects can be counted easily by stopping early.

stem: In the morning a herder keeps one stick for each cow. In the evening she matches each returning cow with one stick, and 3 sticks are left unmatched. What can she conclude?
options: 3 more cows came back than went out
The herd has exactly 3 cows in all
The matching fails, so nothing is known
3 cows have not yet come back home
explanation: Correct option: (D). Each stick stands for one cow that went out, so 3 unmatched sticks mean 3 cows have not returned. Extra cows would leave cows without sticks, not sticks without cows; the total herd is the number of sticks, not 3; and the one-to-one matching works without knowing any number names.

stem: Which statement correctly compares Method 1 (one stick per object) with Method 2 (one letter 'a' to 'z' per object)?
options: Sticks: finite but compact; letters: unending but slow
Both are unending and convenient for large counts
Sticks: unending but bulky; letters: convenient but finite
Letters: unending but bulky; sticks: convenient but finite
explanation: Correct option: (C). Sticks can go on for ever (an unending sequence) but need as many sticks as objects, which is inconvenient for large collections; letters are convenient to say while counting but stop at 26, so they are not unending. The other options swap these properties or claim both methods are unending and convenient, which the chapter shows is false.

stem: The Lebombo bone, discovered in South Africa, is one of the oldest known mathematical artefacts. Which description fits it?
options: About 20,000 years old with 29 notches
About 44,000 years old with 60 notches
About 35,000 years old with 10 notches
About 44,000 years old with 29 notches
explanation: Correct option: (D). The Lebombo bone is a tally stick with 29 notches, estimated to be about 44,000 years old, and may have served as a tally stick or lunar calendar. An age of 20,000 to 35,000 years belongs to the Ishango bone from the Democratic Republic of Congo; 60 and 10 notches are not its count.

stem: In the Gumulgal system, urapon means 1 and ukasar means 2. Which number is 'ukasar-ukasar-urapon'?
explanation: Correct option: (C). ukasar-ukasar-urapon = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5. The number 3 is ukasar-urapon, 4 is ukasar-ukasar, and 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar.

stem: Extending the Gumulgal system beyond 6 by counting in twos, what is (ukasar-ukasar-urapon) + (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon)?
options: ukasar written six times
ukasar written five times, then urapon
ukasar written seven times
ukasar written six times, then urapon
explanation: Correct option: (A). The first number is 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 and the second is 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 7, so the sum is 12. Without number names: the two urapons pair up into one more ukasar, giving 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 ukasars and no urapon left. Five ukasars with urapon is 11, seven ukasars is 14, and six ukasars with urapon is 13.

stem: Why might people using tally marks have replaced every group of 5 marks with a new symbol?
options: Five was thought to be a sacred number
Bones were too short for over five marks
Groups of 5 or more are hard to see at a glance
Five marks were needed to show every day of a week
explanation: Correct option: (C). Most people find it difficult to know the size of a group of 5 or more objects in a single glance, so grouping marks in fives with a new symbol makes the count easy to read, as in the Roman system. The chapter gives no religious reason; bones such as the Lebombo bone carry many more than five marks; and a week does not have five days.

stem: A number system counts only in groups of 5, using one symbol for 1 and one symbol for 5. How many symbols are needed, at the least, to write 1345 in it?
explanation: Correct option: (B). 1345 = 5 x 269 + 0, so it needs 269 symbols for 5 and no symbol for 1, that is 269 symbols. 270 or 274 would come from adding unneeded 1-symbols, and 1345 is the tally count with no grouping at all. Even 269 symbols is cumbersome, which shows why counting in groups of a single size becomes unwieldy for large numbers.

MCCCXXII
MCCXXIII
MMCCXXII

stem: How is 2999 written in Roman numerals, using the 'one less than' form for 900, 90 and 9?
options: MMIM
MMCMIC
MMCMXCIX
MMDCDXCIX

stem: Without converting to Hindu numerals, what is LXXXVII + LXXVIII?
options: CXLV
CLV
CLXXV
CLXV
explanation: Correct option: (D). Collect the symbols: L L = 2 L, X X X X X = 5 X, V V = 2 V, I I I I I = 5 I. Regroup: 5 I = V, so 3 V; 2 V = X with one V left; now 6 X = L + X; and 3 L = C + L. The sum is C L X V = CLXV (87 + 78 = 165). CXLV is 145, CLV is 155 and CLXXV is 175, from regrouping errors.

stem: Which feature of Roman numerals is the main reason multiplication is difficult in that system?
options: A product of two landmarks may not be a landmark
It has no symbol for any number larger than M
Its landmarks are all powers of a single number
Its symbols must always be read from left to right
explanation: Correct option: (A). Multiplying two numbers means multiplying their landmark numbers, and in the Roman system such a product is often not a landmark: for example V x L = 250 = CCL. So every product must be regrouped in an irregular way. Having M as the largest symbol limits size, not multiplication; Roman landmarks are not all powers of one number (that is what a base system has); and reading direction is not the problem.

stem: Which numbers are the landmark numbers of the Egyptian number system?
explanation: Correct option: (B). In the Egyptian system each landmark number is 10 times the previous one, starting from 1, so the landmark numbers are the powers of 10: 1, 10, 100, 1000, and so on. 1, 5, 10, 50, ... are Roman landmarks; 1, 5, 25, ... are powers of 5 (the base-5 system); and 10, 20, 30, ... are multiples of 10, not powers.

stem: What are the first four landmark numbers of a base-7 number system?
explanation: Correct option: (C). The landmark numbers of a base-n system are the powers of n starting from n^0 = 1, so for base 7 they are 7^0 = 1, 7^1 = 7, 7^2 = 49, 7^3 = 343. 7, 14, 21, 28 are multiples of 7; 7, 49, 343, 2401 leaves out the first landmark 1; and 1, 7, 14, 49 wrongly includes 14.

stem: In the base-5 system with landmark numbers 1, 5, 25 and 125, how is 143 grouped when we take as many of the largest landmark as possible first?
options: five 25s, three 5s and three 1s
one 125, three 25s and three 1s
one 125, one 5 and thirteen 1s
one 125, three 5s and three 1s
explanation: Correct option: (D). 143 - 125 = 18; 18 has no 25, so take three 5s (15), leaving 3 ones: 143 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1. Five 25s add up to 143 too, but five 25s must be regrouped into one 125; one 125 with three 25s is 203; and thirteen 1s should be regrouped into two 5s and three 1s.

stem: Why can no symbol appear 10 or more times when a number is written correctly in Egyptian numerals?
options: Scribes were not allowed to repeat symbols
Ten of a landmark make the next landmark
Each symbol may be repeated at most five times
Numbers above ten were not written down
explanation: Correct option: (B). In a base-10 system, 10 copies of any landmark number equal the next landmark number, so they are always regrouped into one symbol of the next power of 10. There was no rule against repeating symbols (324 uses three symbols for 100); repetition up to nine times is allowed, not just five; and the Egyptians wrote numbers up to a crore.

stem: In the base-5 system created in the chapter, what is a simple rule to multiply any number by 5?
options: Write the whole number five times and then regroup
Add one extra symbol for 1 at the right end
Change each 1-symbol to a 5-symbol, keep the rest
Replace each symbol by the next landmark's symbol
explanation: Correct option: (D). Every landmark number is a power of 5, and 5 x 5^k = 5^(k+1), the next landmark. By the distributive property, multiplying the whole number by 5 multiplies each landmark in it by 5, so each symbol is simply replaced by the symbol of the next landmark. Writing the number five times works but is not a simple rule; adding a 1 changes the value by only 1; and changing only the 1-symbols leaves the larger landmarks unmultiplied.

stem: In later times the Mesopotamian number system became a sexagesimal system. What was its base?
explanation: Correct option: (A). A sexagesimal system is a base-60 system; its influence survives in 1 hour = 60 minutes and 1 minute = 60 seconds. Base 10 is the decimal system of the Egyptians and Hindus, base 20 is close to the Mayan system, and 12 is not mentioned as a Mesopotamian base.

stem: The landmark numbers of the Mayan system began 1, 20, ... What was its third landmark number?
explanation: Correct option: (B). The Mayan third landmark number was 360 rather than 400, which some scholars link to their calendars; this is why the Mayan system is not a true base-20 system. 400 = 20 x 20 is what a true base-20 system would use, 3600 is the Mesopotamian 60 x 60, and 200 is not a Mayan landmark.

stem: Writing each place of a Mesopotamian numeral as a number from 1 to 59, how is 7530 shown, places from left to right?
explanation: Correct option: (C). 7530 = 2 x 3600 + 5 x 60 + 30, because 2 x 3600 = 7200 and 7530 - 7200 = 330 = 5 x 60 + 30. So the places are 2 | 5 | 30. '125 | 30' has the right value (125 x 60 + 30) but 125 is 60 or more and must be regrouped; '7 | 5 | 30' confuses base 60 with base 10; '2 | 30 | 5' puts the 60s and 1s in the wrong places.

stem: Why did the later Mesopotamians begin to use a special placeholder symbol in their numerals?
options: To separate one number from the next in a list
To show where each number ended on a tablet
To stand for the landmark number 60
To mark an empty place and avoid misreading
explanation: Correct option: (D). Blank spaces for missing powers of 60 were hard to keep consistent, so the same numeral could be read in different ways. A placeholder symbol marked an empty place, much like our 0. It did not separate numbers in a list or mark the end of a number (it was used mainly in the middle of numbers), and 60 was shown by position, not by this symbol.

stem: Chinese rod numerals alternated Zong (vertical) and Heng (horizontal) symbols in successive places. What was the most likely purpose of this?
options: To tell adjacent places apart clearly
Because Heng rods stood for fractions
To give odd and even numbers different forms
Because Zong rods could only show up to 5
explanation: Correct option: (A). With only Zong symbols and no clear spacing, the rods for 41 could also be read as 23, 32 or 122. Alternating Zong and Heng makes each new place look different from its neighbour, so adjacent places are easy to tell apart. Heng rods stood for tens, thousands and so on, not fractions; the choice depends on place, not on odd or even numbers; and Zong symbols cover 1 to 9.
